read.plain_summary: Dylan Riley draws on Weber persistently across six argumentative routes — class and estate, political capitalism, domination typology, science and value, historical methodology, and standpoint — while progressively containing Weber within a Gramscian-Marxian framework. His narrow quotations and definitions are generally accurate, but when a local passage is made to carry a larger synthesis, the cited locus typically supports only a component of that synthesis. Among the supplied Weber readers, Riley is selectively consonant with Wright on material closure, with Ganev on categorical distinction, and with Ktenas on situated standpoint — but revisionist on estate politics, on the direction of political capitalism, and on the fact-value problem. The buried decision the dossier forces is whether Riley's adaptations are productive scholarly extensions of Weber or selective appropriations whose reach exceeds their textual warrant, case by case.
read.buried_crux: The dossier carries but never states plainly the question of which Riley-Weber moves are philologically secure and which are selective — the fidelity audit answers this case by case (RW0023 is stretched; RW0085 is fair; RW0088 is selective), but the synthesis sections do not consolidate these verdicts into a reader-facing decision table. The crux hides across the three phase-4 analyses: the engagement analysis names the moves, the fidelity audit grades them, but the reception analysis does not draw the thread together as a ranked typology of secure, productive, and over-extended citations.

read.cumulative_direction: The evidence pushes the reader toward a differentiated verdict: Riley's local uses of Weber are largely defensible, his synthetic enlargements are productive but exceed their textual warrant, and his progressive containment of Weber within a Marxian standpoint framework is explicit by 2026. The brief promised a reception-positioning analysis; the evidence delivers one, but it also discloses an unresolved internal tension (2018 vs. 2025 on estates) that the brief did not anticipate. Counter-evidence (Ganev's alternative political-capitalism reading, Love's inconsistency finding, Ktenas's defence of Weberian anti-speculation) is held in the reception section but not fully foregrounded in the summary.
read.form_capacity: The material fills a 5-section dossier comfortably: the three analytical phases each yield a distinct claim, the fidelity phase splits naturally into secure/selective/unverifiable categories, and the reception phase adds independent intellectual context. A 6th or 7th section would be padding.

spine.thesis: Riley uses Weber as a modular interlocutor across two decades — borrowing distinctions selectively, testing them historically, and progressively subordinating them to a Gramscian-Marxian framework — while his citation practice is accurate at narrow quotations but selective or unverifiable when local passages are made to carry larger synthetic claims.

sections.title: Riley's Weber: Modular Borrowing, Selective Fidelity, Gramscian Frame
sections.subtitle: A philological and reception audit of twelve citing acts across two decades, with a verdict table for future users
executive_summary: Across twelve citing acts from 2003 to 2026, Riley treats Weber as a modular interlocutor rather than a systematic reference point. The early period borrows Weber's differentiation of classes, status groups, and parties to license conceptual space for political society; the middle period puts Weber's patrimonial, charismatic, and legal-rational typologies to direct diagnostic work on Judt's ethics and Trump's rule; the late period progressively subordinates Weber's angle of vision to a Gramscian-Marxian frame, explicitly enclosing Weber's firm-centred standpoint within a Lukácsian synthesis. The through-line is political capitalism and the class/estate distinction, which together carry more citation weight than the five other routes combined, and which are where the most consequential tensions within Riley's corpus arise: his 2018 rejection of estate concepts as a category error for advanced capitalism is not reconciled with his 2025 application of those same concepts to political capitalism's structural reinforcement of estate-type politics.

The fidelity record, checked across twenty-eight indexed citation pairs against five routed Weber witnesses, yields a stable pattern: narrow quotations and declared adaptations are generally accurate or fair. The 2013 imperialism prognosis is verbatim-matched at Economy and Society p. 919; the 2018 patrimonial-office quotation is confirmed at both predicates at pp. 1028–31; the 2024 power definition is word-for-word at p. 53; the 2020 adaptation of Roman imperialist capitalism is announced as adaptation and the cited p. 917 supports the retained mechanism. The gap opens when a local passage is promoted into a system-level argument: the political-society formula extends Weber's differentiation beyond what 'Class, Status, Party' states; the capitalism-suffrage thesis adds a broader affinity proposition the cited parliamentary-function pages do not establish; the broad political-capitalism definition is Weberian in substance but wider than pp. 965–66 support; and the census article's state definition substitutes bureaucratic-infrastructural capacity for Weber's held definition by monopoly of legitimate physical force — the one citation the audit classifies as stretched rather than merely selective. Twelve pairs remain unverifiable at the cited locations, meaning the check cannot settle those attributions in either direction.

Among the supplied independent readers — Wright, Ganev, Ktenas, Bendix, Love, Rundell, and Castoriadis — Riley is analytically consonant on categorical distinctions and revisionist on their explanatory uses. Wright is the closest neighbour on estates and closure but holds, unlike Riley's 2025 thesis, that capitalism systematically erodes the salience of traditional status groups. Ganev's Weberian political capitalism presupposes state weakness and de-bureaucratisation; Riley's mature account requires durable fiscal and monetary agencies that engineer asset-price support — a structural divergence on mechanism despite categorical consonance. Love's philological finding that Weber's use of 'capitalism' was not internally consistent and that tax-farming does not satisfy a market-exchange definition complicates the stable Weberian genealogy Riley and Brenner invoke. On the fact-value problem, Ktenas and Bendix defend Wertfreiheit as a genuine methodological achievement; Riley historicises it as a targeted political move against specific enemies, retaining objective possibilities and the ethic of responsibility while discarding value-pluralism — a narrowing none of the supplied readers explicitly contests but none endorses.

sections.heading: How Riley uses Weber: six routes, one modular logic
paragraphs: Across the supplied collection Riley never gives Weber a fixed address. In the 2003 Lombardy article he places the argument explicitly in a "Gramscian and Weberian tradition" and uses "Class, Status, Party" to establish that political society is irreducible to civil-society interests or the state. {{1}} That is genealogy and permission at once: Weber licenses the conceptual space; Gramsci and the historical data fill it. In 2005 Weber enters only as a parenthetical authority for reconstructing suppressed historical alternatives embedded in historical sequences. {{2}} The Weber citation is methodological scaffolding, not load-bearing wall.

Table 1 maps twelve major citing acts from 2003 to 2026 and makes the modular pattern visible: object cited, citation move, stance, and the analytical job Weber is asked to do in each text. [[table:engagement_pattern_citing_acts]] Reading down the Stance column, "Builds on" dominates the early period, giving way to "Adopts" and then to "Builds on and contains" in the late texts — a slow arc from collaboration toward epistemological circumscription.

The middle period — 2011 to 2020 — is where Weber does the most direct argumentative work. In the Judt essay Riley invokes "Politics as a Vocation" to correct Judt's detached moralism: Weber's actual position treats conviction and responsibility as supplements rather than opposites, a reading Riley pairs with Sartre to argue that both thinkers accepted the tension between ethics and politics rather than dissolving it. In the 2018 Trump essay Riley applies Weber's three forms of rule — the charismatic, the patrimonial, and the bureaucratic — to diagnose Trump as a patrimonial misfit inserted into a legal-rational state, a genuinely qualified adoption that refuses to import the category without reservation. {{3}} And in 2020 Faultlines Riley marks his most consequential adaptation with a careful hedge: "Adapting Weber's concept of Roman 'imperialist capitalism', this could perhaps be termed 'political capitalism'." {{4}} The hedge matters: it distinguishes a declared conceptual transfer from an identity claim.

The late texts — 2022 to 2026 — perform a different operation. Marx approached capitalism from the standpoint of wage labour, Weber from that of the owners of capital. {{5}} This 2026 formulation, the most metatheoretically explicit in the collection, credits Weber's firm-centred angle of vision as "highly revealing" while subordinating it to a Lukácsian synthesis. By this point Weber is no longer primarily a source of distinctions to borrow; he is a bourgeois angle of vision to enclose. The 2025 estate-politics chapter preserves real content from Weber — workers who organise through race, ethnicity, or credentials form what Weber called an "estate" rather than a class {{6}} — but inserts that category into a Marxian theory of exploitation and market interests that Weber's own framework does not supply.

The six routes identified in the analysis — political-society genealogy, historical-sociology methodology, political ethics, imperialism and political capitalism, state and bureaucracy, positivism and intellectuals — are not parallel channels of equal weight. Political capitalism and the class/estate distinction together constitute the through-line that runs from 2003 to 2025 and is where most of the citation work happens. The Gramscian-Marxian framework is not one option among the six; it is the frame within which all six routes operate. Weber supplies distinctions; the framework assigns them explanatory duties.

sections.heading: Political capitalism: from material corrective to estate-politics synthesis, 2013–2025
paragraphs: The concept of political capitalism is the longest unbroken thread in Riley's Weber engagement. It passes through three analytically distinct stages, and the tensions between them are not resolved in the supplied texts.

The first stage is a corrective move against Michael Mann. Writing in 2013, Riley reconstructs Weber's theory of imperialism against Mann's predominantly ideological account: it is true that Weber insisted that inter-state competition was saturated with conflicts over prestige, but he also argued that there was a strong material dynamic to imperialism. {{1}} Riley presents Weber here as evidence in a debate, not as the source of a new category. The reconstruction is accurate — the verbatim prognosis at Economy and Society p. 919 matches the held Weber text exactly — but the broader claim that Weber held a Lenin-Hobson-style declining-profit theory is broader than the cited passage alone can establish.

The second stage is the explicit label-transfer of 2020. In Faultlines Riley adapts Weber's concept of Roman imperialist capitalism, applying it to contemporary profit-oriented activity whose returns derive from direct political power. {{2}} What is significant here is the epistemological self-awareness: Riley writes "could perhaps be termed" rather than asserting an identity. The Weber passage at p. 917 supports the adaptation fairly — it identifies expansionary political power as the basis of profit for tax-farmers, state creditors, and colonial capitalists — but the contemporary economic mechanism Riley has in mind (asset-price inflation, bailouts, state guarantees) is already his own addition.

The third stage arrives in 2025 and the undated Thesis text. Riley and Brenner trace the origins of the term political capitalism to Weber, Gabriel Kolko, and Murray Rothbard, and identify tax-farming as its archetypal historical manifestation. {{3}} The undated essay then attributes to Weber a broader definition: economic activity that is profit-oriented but relies predominantly on political means rather than on productivity-enhancing investment. {{4}} The Weber pages at 965–66 support the tax-farming mechanism; they do not themselves use the phrase political capitalism or establish Weber's terminological priority. The genealogical claim is Weberian in substance but selective relative to the cited locus — a gap the fidelity audit makes precise.

Running alongside this trajectory is the class/estate revision, which constitutes an unresolved internal tension. The 2025 estate chapter argues that political capitalism structurally reinforces estate-type politics rather than class politics, making the Weberian category load-bearing for a contemporary diagnosis. But Riley's 2018 Bourdieu critique had explicitly rejected applying the conceptual apparatus of estate-type groups to advanced capitalism as a category error. The two positions are not reconciled in the supplied texts. They could be reconciled — 2018 may be rejecting estates as a general class model, while 2025 applies them to specific fractions under a particular regime — but the later text performs no such reconciliation. The reader who wants to use Riley's estate thesis should treat the 2018 reservation as an open question, not a superseded one.

sections.heading: Citation fidelity: what the Weber pages actually say
paragraphs: Checking Riley's citations against five routed Weber witnesses and twenty-eight indexed pairs yields a stable verdict pattern: direct quotations and narrow definitions generally hold; declared adaptations remain fair when the transformation is announced; and problems arise specifically when a local passage is made to carry a wider synthesis. One citation stands alone as stretched rather than selective.

Table 2 gives every checked pair: Riley's attribution, the verdict, the reason, and the Weber witness anchor. [[table:fidelity_audit_pairs]] Six pairs earn the verdict accurate, four fair, five selective, one stretched, and twelve unverifiable. Read across the Reason column and a single distinction structures the record: whether the citation asks Weber's page to do the job of the page, or the job of an argument that lives several steps beyond it.

The clearest accurate results are at the narrowest citation acts. Riley's 2013 quotation of Weber's imperialism prognosis — "For the predictable future, the prognosis will have to be made in its favor" — matches the held Economy and Society p. 919 word for word. {{1}} The 2018 Trump essay quotes Weber on patrimonial office — the absence of separation between the private and the official sphere, and staff commitment as personal loyalty rather than impersonal rule — and both predicates are confirmed at pp. 1028–31. The 2024 relational-power chapter reproduces Weber's definition of power as the probability an actor carries out its will despite resistance, which the held p. 53 confirms verbatim. These are text-to-text matches.

The declared adaptations hold for a different reason. In Faultlines Riley explicitly writes that he is adapting the Roman concept, and the held p. 917 confirms that Weber identifies the direct exploitation of expansionary political power as the profit basis for the relevant actors. In the 2025 estate chapter Riley compresses Weber's criteria — special esteem, possible monopolies, and the life-conduct requirements of Stand — but preserves class/estate nonidentity and the possibility of a material foundation. Compression of a fairly stated criterion is different from substituting a wrong one.

The selective verdicts mark a coherent practice of local enlargement. The 2003 political-society formula asks Weber's differentiation of classes, status groups, and parties to carry the broader claim that political society is reducible neither to civil-society interests nor to the state; Weber's passage differentiates the spheres without stating Riley's full mediating-domain formula. The capitalism-suffrage thesis in the 2015 Bourdieu article asks the parliamentary-function pages (pp. 1407–10) to establish the affinity of industrial capitalism, mass suffrage, and a strengthened representative state; those pages defend parliament through consent, accountability, and leadership selection, which supports one component but not the full affinity proposition. The 2024 information-dependence claim redirects Weber's genuine insight about bureaucratic information into a general elite-dependence-on-subordinates thesis; Weber's immediate object is bureaucracy's advantage over parliamentary supervisors, not a theory of downward organisational dependence. The tax-farming genealogy and the broad political-capitalism definition are selective for a related reason: Economy and Society pp. 965–66 establishes the mechanism but does not itself use the term political capitalism or state Weber's priority in deploying it.

The sole stretched verdict — the 2015 census article's state definition — is materially different in kind. Riley attributes to Weber a definition of the state in terms of organisational means, specifically its bureaucratic and infrastructural capacities. {{2}} The held Weber pages at pp. 77–78 define the modern state through its successful claim to monopoly of legitimate physical force within a territory. Infrastructural capacity is not the defining predicate at the cited location; this is a substitution, not an enlargement. Twelve pairs remain unverifiable because retrieval reached editorial matter, a different German collection, or an unheld work. Unverifiable does not mean wrong; it means the check cannot settle the question.

The overall pattern confirms the thesis's fidelity claim with precision: narrow quotations and declared adaptations are generally accurate or fair; the gap opens when a local passage is promoted into a system-level argument.

sections.heading: Riley among Weber's readers: consonances, contrasts, and the two fault lines
paragraphs: The supplied independent readers — Wright, Ganev, Ktenas, Bendix, Love, Rundell, Castoriadis, and Swedberg — do not form a school, and none of them cites Riley. What the comparison yields is not a record of influence but a map of analytical consonances and contrasts that allows the researcher to place Riley's Weber moves in a wider interpretive field.

Table 3 positions Riley and each supplied reader on three fault-line themes: estate politics under advanced capitalism, the causal route of political capitalism, and the fact-value problem. [[table:reception_positioning_readers]] The table makes two structural features visible: on categorical distinctions Riley is generally consonant with the supplied readers; on the explanatory uses of those distinctions he is often revisionist, sometimes in ways that contradict his own earlier positions.

On estates and social closure, Wright is the closest analytic neighbour. He preserves a strict class/status distinction, treats status honour as materially consequential through coercive exclusion mechanisms, and recognises the economic rationality of racial closure — all points Riley's 2025 chapter endorses. {{1}} But Wright also argues that both Marx and Weber saw capitalism as systematically eroding the salience of traditional status groups. {{2}} Riley's 2025 thesis runs in the opposite direction: political capitalism structurally reinforces estate-type politics rather than class politics. {{3}} The divergence is not Wright's criticism of Riley; it is an analytical contrast between two independent research trajectories. The sharper internal tension is within Riley's own corpus. His 2018 Bourdieu critique rejected applying estate-type concepts to advanced capitalism as a category error; his 2025 chapter applies those concepts directly to advanced political capitalism. The supplied texts do not reconcile these two positions.

On political capitalism, Ganev provides the most sustained independent Weberian reconstruction. He sharply distinguishes rational acquisition of profits from political capitalism as contrasting analytical categories, and locates political capitalism in social and institutional disarray — de-bureaucratisation, unmonitorable discretion, and the collapse of legal-administrative routines. {{4}} Riley's mature account moves in a different direction: contemporary political capitalism depends on durable, capable fiscal and monetary agencies that systematically engineer asset-price support. Ganev's postcommunist political capitalism presupposes state weakness; Riley's requires state effectiveness. The two are consonant on the categorical point — market acquisition and political extraction are analytically distinct — and divergent on the empirical mechanism. Love adds a further complication: he shows that Weber's own use of the term capitalism was not consistent, and that tax-farming does not satisfy a market-exchange definition of capitalism. This challenges the stable Weberian anchor that Riley and Brenner invoke for their tax-farming genealogy.

On the fact-value problem, Ktenas defends Wertfreiheit as a genuine methodological achievement: the person who inquires from a value-laden standpoint plays an active and creative role without being able to present just anything as valid. {{5}} Bendix presents Weber's exclusion of political value judgments from academic teaching as compatible with passionate commitment to impartiality outside the classroom. Riley's 2023 Brown review takes a harder line: Weber's sundering of fact and value was a political move aimed at specific enemies — Marxist scientific socialism and German nationalism — and he illicitly extended his problem to values in general. {{6}} Riley retains the concept of objective possibilities from Weber and keeps the ethic of responsibility, but the broader value-pluralism is historicised away. Ktenas and Bendix defend a position Riley narrows; none of the supplied texts argues explicitly against Riley's reconstruction.

Rundell offers a consonance on institutional pluralism. His medieval autonomous city exists outside the orbit of the patrimonial state, and groups figurate the political from positions of closure and circumscription — a structural logic parallel to Riley's argument that political organisation independently constrains class formation. The substantive objects differ entirely — medieval Italian city-states versus contemporary Trumpian rule or Lombard patricians — and no demonstrated engagement connects the two readings. The consonance is analytical, not intellectual-historical.

sections.heading: Decision table: which Riley–Weber moves to trust, track, or check independently
paragraphs: The fidelity and reception evidence together resolve into three categories that a researcher should treat differently. They are not a hierarchy of quality; they are a map of epistemic risk.

The first category — secure moves — contains narrow quotations and declared adaptations where the Weber text establishes what Riley claims. The 2013 imperialism prognosis is verbatim-matched. {{1}} The 2018 patrimonial office quotation is confirmed at both predicates. The 2024 power definition is word-for-word. The ethic of responsibility reconstruction is fair, supported by Weber's requirement that an actor give an account of the foreseeable results of one's action. The 2020 adaptation of Roman imperialist capitalism is declared as adaptation, not identity, and the cited p. 917 supports the retained mechanism. The estate application preserves class/estate nonidentity with a Weberian foundation even under compression. A researcher can cite these Riley moves with confidence, though always with the qualification that application to contemporary objects is Riley's own work, not Weber's.

The second category — productive but selective moves — contains attributions where the cited locus supports a genuine Weberian component but not the full claim Riley builds on it. The political-society formula extends Weber's differentiation beyond what "Class, Status, Party" states. The capitalism-suffrage thesis adds to Weber's parliamentary-function argument a wider affinity proposition the cited pages do not establish. The information-dependence claim redirects a genuine bureaucratic insight into a general theory of elite dependence on subordinates. The tax-farming genealogy confirms the mechanism but not terminological priority. The broad political-capitalism definition is Weberian in substance but wider than pp. 965–66 establish. Riley's Weber is doing real work in all these moves; it simply does not do all the work the argument assigns it. A researcher who uses these moves should track the Weberian component separately from Riley's synthesis, verify what the cited pages actually contain, and treat the larger claim as Riley's contribution with Weberian materials — a productive adaptation, not a textually licensed assertion.

The third category — moves requiring independent retrieval — contains the stretched state definition and the twelve unverifiable pairs. The census article attributes to Weber a definition of the state in terms of bureaucratic and infrastructural capacities, but the held pages define the state through monopoly of legitimate physical force. {{2}} That substitution is material: a researcher who builds on Riley's state-centred argument should retrieve Weber's pp. 77–78 before citing. Weber's own claim that there are no general laws of history is itself a theory of history — and is contradicted by his own theory of rationalization: {{3}} this attribution is used as a foil but has no routed primary locus in the supplied materials. The four Relational Power Theory polarities (formal/informal, cooperative/conflictual, people-as-power-holders, and the managerial-direction-for-profit claim) are unverifiable at their cited pages. Riley and Brenner's genealogy of political capitalism names Weber as the term's origin, but the cited pages establish tax-farming as Historically its archetypal manifestation without using the term or establishing priority. {{4}} For all of these, the rule is simple: go to Weber before citing Riley's attribution.

Two open questions frame the limits of this audit. First, does another Weber locus state the broad political-capitalism definition — profit through political rather than productivity-enhancing means — more directly than pp. 965–66? The supplied witnesses do not settle it. Second, does Riley's 2025 estate-politics thesis reconcile with his 2018 rejection of estate concepts for advanced capitalism, or does it constitute a revision without acknowledgement? The supplied texts establish the tension; they do not dissolve it. A future reader who engages Riley's political-capitalism and estate-politics theses together should treat the 2018 reservation as an active methodological question, not a closed one.

conclusion: Philologically secure moves — cite with confidence, noting that application to contemporary objects is Riley's own work: the 2013 imperialism prognosis (verbatim, p. 919), the 2018 patrimonial-office quotation (confirmed at both predicates, pp. 1028–31), the 2024 power definition (word-for-word, p. 53), the ethic of responsibility reconstruction (fair, Weber's own foreseeable-results criterion), and the 2020 Roman imperialist capitalism adaptation (declared as adaptation, mechanism confirmed at p. 917).

Productive but selective moves — track the Weberian component separately from Riley's synthesis and verify what the cited pages contain before treating the larger claim as textually licensed: the political-society formula (Weber differentiates the spheres; the full mediating-domain thesis is Riley's addition), the capitalism-suffrage thesis (the parliamentary-function pages support one component, not the full affinity proposition), the information-dependence claim (redirects a genuine bureaucratic insight into a broader elite-dependence theory), and the political-capitalism genealogy (tax-farming mechanism confirmed, terminological priority and the broad profit-through-political-means definition not established at pp. 965–66).

Moves requiring independent retrieval before citation: go to Weber's pp. 77–78 before using Riley's state definition, because the held pages define the state through monopoly of legitimate physical force, not bureaucratic-infrastructural capacity — a material substitution, not a selective enlargement. For the twelve unverifiable pairs, retrieve the cited Weber location and settle the attribution independently. And treat two open questions as active rather than closed: whether another Weber locus establishes the broad political-capitalism definition more directly than pp. 965–66, and whether Riley's 2025 estate-politics thesis constitutes a silent revision of his 2018 rejection of estate concepts for advanced capitalism — a tension the supplied texts establish but do not dissolve.
sections.summary_job_met: The summary states the overall finding — Riley's engagement is persistent, modular, and progressively Gramscian — in the body's proportions across the political-capitalism thread, the fidelity audit results, and the reception comparison, with all qualifications (unverifiable pairs, the stretched state definition, the internal 2018/2025 tension) preserved, so a busy researcher can assess the argument without reading further.
sections.conclusion_job_met: The close supplies a three-category decision rule — secure, productive-but-selective, and requiring independent retrieval — that is entirely distinct from the summary's findings, naming the specific citation pairs and Weber page locations a researcher must act on, and designating the two unresolved open questions as active methodological obligations rather than settled matters.

crosscheck.summary: The dossier is intellectually coherent and its thesis is well-supported by the evidence marshalled, but three structural problems prevent a clean verdict. First, Section 6 ("What this means") is a near-verbatim restatement of Section 5's decision table — redundant summary masquerading as a conclusion with its own job. Second, the spine specifies a 27-citing-text corpus but the dossier opens with "twelve citing acts" and Table 1 lists twelve rows — a number drift that will mislead any reader who checks the methods against the claim. Third, anchor em:EJJLVCUC (Section 5/6, rationalization-as-theory-of-history foil) is cited in prose as a load-bearing claim but has no routed primary Weber locus — an unbacked claim used as argumentative evidence, not merely colour.
crosscheck.what_changed: No standing findings were carried into this review. All findings above are new.

findings.quote: Philologically secure moves — cite with confidence, noting that application to contemporary objects is Riley's own work: the 2013 imperialism prognosis (verbatim, p. 919), the 2018 patrimonial-office quotation (confirmed at both predicates, pp. 1028–31), the 2024 power definition (word-for-word, p. 53), the ethic of responsibility reconstruction (fair, Weber's own foreseeable-results criterion), a
findings.note: Section 6 ('What this means') repeats Section 5's three-category decision table almost sentence for sentence — secure moves, productive-but-selective moves, moves requiring independent retrieval — without adding interpretive stakes or a decision rule not already present in Section 5. A reader who has read Section 5 gains nothing from Section 6 except repetition. The spine assigns Section 6 a distinct job: supply the decision rule for future readers, distinguishing philologically secure from productive-adaptive from check-independently moves. That job is discharged in Section 5; Section 6 should either be merged into Section 5 as its closing paragraph or rewritten to deliver the interpretive stakes the summary calls for (what the fidelity and reception record means for how Weber scholarship should treat Riley).
findings.realization: Fold Section 6 into the close of Section 5. Replace the current Section 6 text with a single paragraph that names the decision rule's interpretive stakes: 'The three-category map above carries one broader implication for Weber scholarship: Riley's corpus demonstrates that modular, instrumental citation of a canonical theorist can be both analytically productive and philologically slippery within a single text. The secure moves show that instrumental use does not preclude accuracy; the selective moves show that accuracy at the locus does not guarantee accuracy at the synthesis level. Future readers of either Riley or Weber should treat this record as a general model for auditing secondary use of primary theoretical sources — checking not only whether the quoted words match but whether the quoted page can carry the argumentative load placed on it.'

findings.quote: Across the supplied collection Riley never gives Weber a fixed address.
findings.note: The spine specifies 27 citing texts; the Summary states 'twelve citing acts'; Table 1 has twelve rows; and the body of Section 1 says 'twelve major citing acts.' The number 27 appears nowhere in the dossier body, yet the thesis — which researchers will quote — names it as the corpus size. A reader checking methods will find 12 ≠ 27 and cannot tell whether the spine's 27 is an error, refers to a wider corpus from which 12 representative acts were selected, or was silently revised downward. The discrepancy should be resolved: either the thesis should be revised to '12 major citing acts drawn from a corpus of 27 citing texts' (if 12 are a representative sample), or every occurrence of 12 should be updated to 27 (if Table 1 is incomplete).
findings.realization: In the Summary, change 'twelve citing acts from 2003 to 2026' to 'twelve major citing acts, selected from a corpus of 27 citing texts spanning 2003 to 2026.' In Section 1 paragraph 1, change 'twelve major citing acts' to 'twelve major citing acts (drawn from a 27-text corpus).' Add a note to Table 1's header: 'Table 1 represents twelve major citing acts selected from a corpus of 27 citing texts; the full corpus index is reported in the supplementary citation log.' This preserves the spine's stated N while making the sampling logic transparent to a methodologically attentive reader.

findings.quote: Weber's own claim that there are no general laws of history is itself a theory of history — and is contradicted by his own theory of rationalization
findings.note: This sentence appears in Section 5 as an example of a move 'requiring independent retrieval' — and anchor em:EJJLVCUC is cited for it — but the audit's own verdict for this citation is that 'this attribution is used as a foil but has no routed primary locus in the supplied materials.' The dossier therefore uses an unverifiable attribution as evidence in its own argument: the claim that Riley uses Weber as a foil is backed only by a Riley text making the claim, with no Weber witness confirming what Weber actually said. For a document aimed at researchers who are told to 'cite the documents exactly,' deploying an unverified attribution as a positive example (of the 'moves requiring retrieval' category) without flagging its own unverifiability is self-undermining. The sentence should be rewritten to make explicit that the attribution is itself unverifiable in the supplied materials.
findings.realization: Replace the current sentence with: 'Riley uses Weber's claimed denial of general historical laws as a foil — attributing to Weber the position that his rationalization theory itself refutes (anchor em:EJJLVCUC) — but the supplied Weber witnesses do not recover the primary locus for Weber's denial of general laws, making this attribution itself a case of the unverifiable category: a researcher should retrieve the Weber passage before citing Riley's foil as established.' This makes the example self-consistent with the audit's own unverifiable verdict.

findings.quote: Riley's 2013 quotation of Weber's imperialism prognosis — 'For the predictable future, the prognosis will have to be made in its favor' — matches the held Economy and Society p. 919 word for word.
findings.note: Anchor em:PSYPHAPS (used for the imperialism-prognosis accuracy claim throughout Sections 1, 2, 3, and 5) quotes Riley's own text — 'It is true that Weber insisted that inter-state competition was saturated with conflicts over prestige. But he also argued that there was a strong material dynamic to imperialism' — not a Weber witness. The verbatim match claim is made in the prose ('matches the held Economy and Society p. 919 word for word') and in Table 2 (RW0016, verdict: Accurate), but the anchor supplied for the accuracy claim is Riley's paraphrase, not the retrieved Weber page. The fidelity column in Table 2 correctly leaves the Weber witness anchor cell for RW0016 blank (no text given), which is consistent — but the body text presents the accuracy finding as though the anchor confirms it, when the anchor only confirms Riley's claim. This is not a misattribution but a gap in evidentiary presentation: the prose assertion of verbatim match is backed by a Riley anchor, not a Weber anchor. For a researcher audience, this distinction matters. The prose should note that the Weber witness for RW0016 was not recovered in the supplied routing but that the Table 2 note records the verdict
findings.realization: In Section 3, revise the sentence to: 'Riley's 2013 quotation of Weber's imperialism prognosis — "For the predictable future, the prognosis will have to be made in its favor" — is recorded in Table 2 (RW0016) as accurate; the Weber witness anchor for this pair is not among the five routed witnesses, but the quotation is placed within quotation marks in Riley's text and the cited locus (E&S p. 919) is identified precisely enough that independent retrieval can settle the match directly.'

findings.quote: Six pairs earn the verdict accurate, four fair, five selective, one stretched, and twelve unverifiable.
findings.note: This sentence appears in the body prose immediately after Table 2. Table 2's own note reads: 'Direct quotations and narrow definitions (RW0016, RW0042, RW0050, RW0064, RW0076, RW0084) consistently hold' — six pairs, accurate — and lists selective and other verdicts. The prose sentence essentially restates the table's note tally. A researcher reading the table gets the count from the note; the prose sentence adds no interpretive argument, only a recount. More importantly, the prose should be doing the analytical work (what the pattern means for the thesis), while the caption/note carries the count. The prose sentence should be revised to lead with interpretation rather than restatement.
findings.realization: Replace 'Six pairs earn the verdict accurate, four fair, five selective, one stretched, and twelve unverifiable.' with: 'The distribution of verdicts — six accurate, four fair, five selective, one stretched, twelve unverifiable — is less significant than its internal structure: accurate and fair verdicts cluster at the narrowest citation acts (direct quotation, declared adaptation), while selective and stretched verdicts cluster at system-level arguments that ask a local passage to do more than it states. The unverifiable block, at nearly half the checked pairs, sets a ceiling on what the audit can settle without fuller access to the Weber corpus.'

findings.quote: The table makes two structural features visible: on categorical distinctions Riley is generally consonant with the supplied readers; on the explanatory uses of those distinctions he is often revisionist, sometimes in ways that contradict his own earlier positions.
findings.note: Section 4 introduces Table 3 with a pointer that reads correctly ('Table 3 positions Riley and each supplied reader on three fault-line themes'). However, the Castoriadis and Swedberg rows that appear in the spine's commissioned description ('supplied independent readers — Wright, Ganev, Ktenas, Bendix, Love, Rundell, Castoriadis, and Swedberg') are entirely absent from Table 3 as rendered. Castoriadis and Swedberg are named in the section's opening sentence as 'supplied independent readers' but receive no rows and no prose discussion. A researcher following the reader list will look for them and find nothing — creating the impression of an incomplete or selectively rendered table. Either rows for Castoriadis and Swedberg should be added (if they carry positions on the three fault-line themes), or the opening sentence should be revised to remove their names from the list of readers whose positions are mapped.
findings.realization: Option A (preferred if the witnesses carry relevant content): Add two rows to Table 3. Row 1 — Reader: Castoriadis; Theme: fact–value / intellectual standpoint; Position on Weber: [retrieve from supplied Castoriadis witness]; Relation to Riley: [state consonance or contrast]. Row 2 — Reader: Swedberg; Theme: political capitalism / categorical distinctions; Position on Weber: [retrieve from supplied Swedberg witness]; Relation to Riley: [state consonance or contrast]. Option B (if the witnesses do not carry relevant positions on the three fault lines): Revise the opening sentence of Section 4 to: 'The supplied independent readers — Wright, Ganev, Ktenas, Bendix, Love, and Rundell — do not form a school, and none of them cites Riley.' Remove Castoriadis and Swedberg from the list to match Table 3's actual coverage.

findings.quote: By this point Weber is no longer primarily a source of distinctions to borrow; he is a bourgeois angle of vision to enclose.
findings.note: The term 'Einkesselung' (Lukácsian encirclement/enclosure) is invoked in Table 3's note ('endorses Lukácsian Einkesselung of Weber') as though it is a technical term the researcher audience will recognize, but it is never glossed in the text. The prose uses 'enclose' and 'subordinate' as functional equivalents but does not explain that Einkesselung is Lukács's term for dialectically surrounding and superseding a partial perspective by situating it within a totalising standpoint. For a researcher audience that is 'precise and methodologically explicit,' the unglossed use of a German technical term in a table note — while the body uses only the English approximation — is an inconsistency: either gloss it in the body the first time 'enclose' appears, or use it in the body and gloss it there.
findings.realization: At the first use of 'enclose' in the body of Section 1 (the sentence 'he is a bourgeois angle of vision to enclose'), add a parenthetical gloss: '— enclose in the Lukácsian sense of Einkesselung: situating a partial standpoint within a totalising perspective that reveals both its insight and its limits —'. In Table 3's note, replace 'endorses Lukácsian Einkesselung of Weber' with 'endorses what Lukács called Einkesselung (encirclement) of Weber's standpoint: crediting its revelatory power while subordinating it to the wage-labour perspective as the epistemically privileged vantage point on capitalism as a totality.'
